title: Value of Wellness Ratings and Countermovement Jumping Velocity to Monitor Performance
authors: Michael T. Brasch, Kevin L. Neeld, Kristen F. Konkol and Robert W. Pettitt
scope: Original study of 30 male NCAA Division II baseball players during a six-week offseason program.
adds: A baseball example of training structure, repeated testing and disagreement between subjective wellness and an instrumented jump metric.
limitations: Small, single-program collegiate sample. Mean concentric velocity was measured with a linear transducer; results do not establish the performance of every force-plate metric. This was not a professional-baseball readiness or injury-prediction validation.
recommendedUse: Read alongside the reliability and monitoring assignments. Critique the measurement protocol before interpreting a change; compare a study's schedule with the constraints of a professional season.
exactSections: Methods: Participants, Protocol and Statistical Analysis, printed pp. 90–92 (pp. 3–5).
Results, printed pp. 92–95 (pp. 5–8); Tables 1–2 on printed pp. 94–95.

title: Using Biomechanical Devices in Elite Baseball Pitchers: A Preliminary Feasibility Study
authors: Chelsea L. Martin, Kelly R. Evenson, Justin B. Moore, et al.
scope: Prospective feasibility research with 22 collegiate summer-league pitchers; despite the title, this is not an MLB cohort.
adds: Operational definitions for device uptake, continued use, eligible opportunities and missingness. Shows why a technically attractive monitoring system still needs a workable collection process.
limitations: Small sample, device-specific implementation, and no game sleeve use. Numerical reporting differs between abstract/results/discussion; this resource map deliberately avoids adopting its percentages. It does not establish injury prevention or device validity.
recommendedUse: Design an adherence dashboard and data-collection plan. Specify who records each measure, when it is collected, the denominator, missing-data reasons and who acts on the result.
exactSections: Methods: Study Design and Description of Biomechanical Devices and Data Collection, pp. 2–3.
Main Outcomes: Uptake and Adherence; Statistical Analyses, p. 3.

title: Statcast Search CSV Documentation
scope: Official field definitions and units for publicly available Statcast Search downloads.
adds: A real baseball data dictionary for player identifiers, event dates, pitch and batted-ball variables. Documents tracking-era differences and deprecated fields.
limitations: Observed game data omit bullpen and other untracked exposure, medical status, recovery and internal load. A measurement is not an injury-risk score. Definitions can change; document retrieval date, filters and units for every analysis.
recommendedUse: After the synthetic assignments, export a small dated search from Baseball Savant and reproduce the same audit workflow: identify rows, check missingness, separate pitch types and report uncertainty. No player medical inference.
exactSections: game_date, pitcher, batter, game_pk, at_bat_number and pitch_number.
plate_x and plate_z: documented 2026 measurement-location change; deprecated fields.

title: The Effect of Specific Strength Training on Throwing Velocity in Overarm Throwing: A Systematic Review
authors: Andrea Bao Fredriksen and Roland van den Tillaar
scope: Seventeen intervention studies across overarm sports; predominantly handball, with only two baseball studies.
adds: A comparative map of weighted implements, forearm loading, pulley devices and resistance-band work, including intervention/control comparisons.
limitations: Cross-sport transfer is a major constraint. Heterogeneous populations and protocols, small evidence groups, and uncertain injury implications prevent a universal baseball prescription. General strength training was excluded. The authors' mechanistic explanations are not all directly tested.
recommendedUse: Practice evidence appraisal: distinguish within-group improvement from superiority to a control, identify which rows are baseball, and explain why a velocity result alone cannot settle safety or program choice.
exactSections: Methods: Experimental Approach to the Problem and Inclusion Criteria.
Results and Tables 1–3: sport, sample and intervention comparisons.
Discussion: learning effects, possible overlapping samples, generalizability; Conclusion.

title: The Weight Room Builds Athletes. The Field Builds Baseball Players. Train Adaptations, Not Exercises
scope: Public coaching perspective from a practitioner with professional baseball experience; posted September 8, 2026.
adds: A useful exercise-selection discussion: name the physical adaptation sought and connect physical preparation with baseball skill practice.
limitations: Expert opinion, not an intervention study or complete periodized program. Broad exercise judgments and performance or durability claims need independent appraisal; strength transfer is not guaranteed.
recommendedUse: For each exercise in a programming case, state the target quality, expected progression, coaching requirement and how transfer will be evaluated. Compare the argument with a strength and conditioning textbook chapter on exercise selection.
exactSections: Strength Is the Foundation; Don't Confuse Training with Practice.
Build the Athlete First; The Takeaways.

title: NSCA Strength and Conditioning Professional Standards and Guidelines
scope: General strength and conditioning operations; the 24-page document linked from NSCA's position-statements page at the access check.
adds: A framework for staffing, instruction, facility operations, documentation, medical handoffs and emergency preparation that complements exercise programming.
limitations: Published in 2017 and not specific to baseball. It is not a substitute for current local law, credential requirements, employer policy or venue-specific procedures. Access today does not make every detail newly updated.
recommendedUse: Build an affiliate operating checklist and a clear handoff record. Use its operational categories to identify questions for the employing organization, rather than treating one checklist as universal compliance.
exactSections: Emergency Planning and Response; Records and Record Keeping, printed/pp. 7–8 and 12.
Appendix 3: Strength and Conditioning Performance Team Development, printed/p. 16.
